text: Every nightly job eventually fails for some reason. This video decides, on paper, exactly what happens when that occurs — before it happens live, at 2am, with nobody watching.

Five realistic failure modes, not just "something might break": a missing file, a malformed file, a row referencing a product that doesn't exist yet, a missed checkpoint, or the job accidentally running twice.

Two principles decide the handling for all five. Idempotency: re-running the load for a given date can never create duplicate sales — the fix for most failures is "fix the input, re-run," and that has to be safe.

And fail-loud-not-silent: every failure mode produces a visible, logged, alerted event. A job that reports success while quietly having skipped a store is the worst outcome on this list — worse than an honest failure.

A missing file doesn't block the other thirteen stores — it logs which one, alerts a human, loads what did arrive. An unresolved product gets redirected to a review table, never silently dropped, never silently inserted with a blank key.

All of this gets built around one table, etl_run_log, that every stage writes to before this series even opens SSIS. It's the single table that makes a future diagnosis — the bug we chase down in video seventeen — possible after the fact.

The whole philosophy fits in one sentence: a failed or partial load should be loud, logged, and safe to re-run — never invisible, never duplicated. That sentence is the test every design decision from here through the SSIS build gets checked against. Next: SQL Server Management Studio finally opens.
